bib.title: Foundations of Probability (Chapter 2 of Bandit Algorithms)

question: What measure-theoretic probability does the rest of the bandit book need, and how can it be introduced through intuition rather than a list of definitions?
contributions: A non-standard introduction to probability spaces, random elements, sigma-algebras as knowledge, filtrations, conditional probability, independence, integration and conditional expectation, with notes on Radon-Nikodym derivatives and Fubini.

results.claim: In the dice game, all seven dice are rolled up front so the outcome space is {1..6}^7 and each outcome has equal probability.
results.metric: probability of one outcome in Omega
results.setup: Game: roll a die; on a four roll two dice next, else one; three rounds; payoff is the sum of faces; at most seven dice needed. Fair dice.

results.claim: Conditional expectation of a die roll X given Y = I{X>3} is a random variable: 5Y + 2(1-Y).
The product of two copies of 2^{1,2} has only 10 measurable rectangles, versus 16 sets in the product sigma-algebra, so F1 x F2 differs from sigma(F1 x F2).
results.setup: F1=F2=2^{1,2}; six sets are missing from the rectangles.

results.claim: Taking the limit q=p+eps for Y uniform on [0,1] and X Bernoulli(Y) gives E[X|Y in [p,q]]=(p+q)/2 and, in the limit, P(X=1|Y=p)=p; this does not generalise to abstract spaces, which motivates the sigma-algebra definition.
results.setup: Y~Uniform[0,1], X in {0,1} Bernoulli with bias Y.

results.claim: There is no measure on ([0,1], power set) assigning length b-a to every interval, so the sigma-algebra cannot always be the power set (Theorem 2.3).
results.quote: there does not exist a measure P on (Ω, F) such that P([a, b]) = b −a

results.claim: Filtration F_t = sigma(X_1:t) is nested and models the learner's growing knowledge; F_0 is the trivial algebra whose measurable functions are constants.
Expectation of a sum equals the sum of expectations even when the terms are dependent (Proposition 2.6), but E[XY]=E[X]E[Y] needs independence.
results.setup: E[sum |X_i|] must exist for the first; X,Y independent and integrable for the second.
results.quote: This exchange of expectations and summation is the source of much magic

results.claim: Tower rule: if G1 is contained in G2 then E[X|G1]=E[E[X|G2]|G1] a.s.
results.quote: If G1 ⊆G2, then E [X | G1] = E [E [X | G2] | G1] almost surely.

limits: Pure background: no experiments, no algorithms, no bandit setting appears in the chapter.
Authors concede that 'sigma(X) contains all information about X' is not exactly true; it fails for coarse range sigma-algebras or non-measurable f (Exercise 2.6).
Factorisation lemma needs a Borel space; the definition is deferred to the next chapter.
Dominated/monotone convergence, Fatou and Jensen are not covered (Jensen is deferred to Chapter 26).
Authors say a great deal of the book can be read without the chapter, taking results on faith.
practices: Separate the source of randomness (Omega) from the mechanism that maps it to values; the choice of Omega is far from unique and does not matter (Sec 2.1, Note 3).
Check independence assumptions against the physical process being modelled; it is a modelling choice, not a mathematical one (Sec 2.4).
Represent what a learner knows at time t by the sigma-algebra generated by observations so far (a filtration) (Sec 2.2).
State independence of several variables as mutual independence by default (Sec 2.4).
Change P while keeping X fixed to get a different law; the book uses this in lower-bound proofs (Sec 2.1, p.22).
Define conditional expectation via sub-sigma-algebras, since conditioning on a probability-zero event is not well defined (Sec 2.6).

terms.definition: The set Omega of elementary random outcomes; its elements are outcomes.
A set F of subsets of Omega that includes Omega and is closed under complementation and countable unions.
A function P: F -> R with P(Omega)=1, P(A)>=0, P(A^c)=1-P(A) and countable additivity over disjoint sets.
The triplet (Omega, F, P); (Omega, F) alone is a measurable space.
An F/B(R)-measurable function X: Omega -> R; a random element is an F/G-measurable function into an arbitrary measurable space.
P_X(A)=P(X^-1(A)); any probabilistic question about X can be answered from P_X alone.
I_A(w)=1 if w in A, else 0; a random variable iff A is measurable.
A sequence (F_t) of sub-sigma-algebras of F with F_t contained in F_{t+1}.
(X_t) is F-adapted if X_t is F_t-measurable for each t.
(X_t) is F-predictable if X_t is F_{t-1}-measurable for each t; predictable implies adapted.
Events A,B are independent if P(A and B)=P(A)P(B); random variables are independent if sigma(X) and sigma(Y) are.
E[X]=integral of X(w) dP(w), the Lebesgue integral with respect to P.
E[X|H] is any H-measurable g with integral over H of g dP equal to integral over H of X dP for all H in H; E[X|Y]=E[X|sigma(Y)].
X=Y P-a.s. if they agree except on a P-null set (P(U)=0).
dP/dQ, an F-measurable function with P(A)=integral over A of dP/dQ dQ; exists iff P is absolutely continuous w.r.t. Q (Q sigma-finite).
x -> P(X>x); E[X] = integral from 0 to infinity of P(X>x) dx for X>=0.
